title: Conditionals
subtitle: Zero, first, second, third, mixed and inverted conditionals; unless, in case, as/so long as, provided that

rows.use: General or scientific facts and definitions
rows.example: If you **have** faith in something, you **believe** in something you cannot prove.

blocks.text: Form: **if** + a present tense, **will** + bare infinitive

rows.use: Real or likely conditions in the present or future and their results
rows.example: If you **have** a birthday party, you'll **get** lots of cool presents! · If you're **working** till half past six, we'll **have** dinner at about eight. · If you **have revised** properly, you **won't have** any problems in the test next week.

blocks.text: We can also use **may, might, can, could, shall, should, ought to, have to** instead of **will**, depending on the meaning.
blocks.note: If you **have** a birthday party, you **might get** lots of cool presents!

blocks.text: We can also use **should** + bare infinitive instead of present simple. This suggests the situation is possible, but unlikely to happen.
blocks.note: If you **should bump** into Alex at the concert, you'll be able to get a lift home.

blocks.text: We can also use a form of the first conditional to give instructions: **if** + a present tense, imperative.
blocks.note: If you **decide** to have a birthday party, **tell** me!

theory.title: unless, in case, as/so long as, provided (that)

rows.example: I'll be there at six **unless** I get delayed. (= except if I get delayed / if I don't get delayed)
Let's take our wellies **in case** it's muddy. (= because it might be muddy)
**As long as** I'm happy, my parents don't care what job I do. · **So long as** I'm happy, my parents don't care what job I do.
**Provided (that)** I'm happy, my parents don't care what job I do.

blocks.text: Form: **if** + past simple or past continuous, **would** + bare infinitive

rows.use: Impossible, unlikely or hypothetical conditions in the present or future and their results
rows.example: If you **had** a beard, you **would look** just like Charles Dickens! · If you **were flying** to Rio, **would** you **get** there much quicker?
If I **were** you, I **would think** very carefully about my future. (more formal) · If I **was** you, I'd **have** a party at the weekend! (more informal)

blocks.text: We can also use **might** or **could** instead of **would**, depending on the meaning. (**could** here often means **would be able to**.)
blocks.note: If we **were** older, we **could go** on holiday on our own.

blocks.text: We can also use **could** in the **if** clause. Here, it means **was/were able to**.
blocks.note: If I **could drive**, I'd buy a car.

blocks.text: Form: **if** + past perfect (simple or continuous), **would + have + past participle**

rows.use: Hypothetical past conditions and their results in the past
rows.example: If you **had worn** a fake beard, no one **would have known** who you were! · If she'd **been wearing** her new glasses, I **would have noticed** them.

blocks.text: We can also use **might, could** or **should** instead of **would**, depending on the meaning.
blocks.note: If I **had done** some revision, I **might / could / should have passed** the exam.

rows.use: **if** + past perfect, **would** + bare infinitive · hypothetical past condition and a present result
rows.example: If I **had listened** to my parents, I **wouldn't be** in so much trouble now.

rows.use: **if** + past simple or past continuous, **would + have + past participle** · hypothetical present condition and a past result
rows.example: If I **had** a mobile, I **would have called** you last night.

rows.use: More formal first conditional (**Should** I/you/he/etc. … instead of **If** I/you/he/etc. **should** …)
rows.example: **Should** the situation worsen, the United Nations is prepared to send in a peacekeeping force.

rows.use: More formal second conditional (**Were** I/you/he/etc. … instead of **If** I/you/he/etc. **were** …)
rows.example: **Were** the situation to worsen, the United Nations would be prepared to send in a peacekeeping force.

rows.use: More formal third conditional (**Had** I/you/he/etc. … instead of **If** I/you/he/etc. **had** …)
rows.example: **Had** the situation worsened, the United Nations would have been prepared to send in a peacekeeping force.

blocks.text: For all conditional sentences, when the condition comes before the result it is usually followed by a comma. When the result comes first, no comma is necessary.
blocks.note: If I had a mobile, I would have called you last night. · I would have called you last night if I had a mobile.

blocks.text: In conditional sentences, modals (will, would, could, etc.) are sometimes followed by a continuous infinitive.
blocks.note: We'd **still be waiting** if you hadn't turned up.

items: With second and third conditionals in informal conversation, speakers of American English sometimes use **would** or **would have** in the **if** clause. This is very unusual in British English.
US: How **would** you feel if this **happened / would happen** to you?
UK: How **would** you feel if this **happened** to you?
US: I **would have** felt awful if that **had happened / would have happened** to me.
UK: I **would have** felt awful if that **had happened** to me.

exercises.title: A · Yes or No
exercises.instruction: Answer Yes or No about the meaning of each sentence.

items.prompt: If Carl doesn't come to the party, I'll be really upset. Is it possible that Carl won't come to the party?
If my neighbour became prime minister, he'd give everyone a million euros. Is it possible that the neighbour will become prime minister?
If Helen weren't here, I don't know what we'd do. Is Helen here now?
If Tarek had had enough money, he'd have bought a car. Did Tarek have enough money?
If Tarek had had enough money, he'd have bought a car. Did he buy a car?
If Debbie hadn't gone to the UK, she wouldn't have met Will. Did Debbie go to the UK?
If Debbie hadn't gone to the UK, she wouldn't have met Will. Did she meet Will?
If the police had investigated the case thoroughly, they wouldn't have arrested Keren. Did the police investigate the case thoroughly?
If the police had investigated the case thoroughly, they wouldn't have arrested Keren. Did they arrest Keren?
Had she not gone to university, she might not have started her own business. Did she go to university?
Had she not gone to university, she might not have started her own business. Did she start her own business?

exercises.title: J · Extra word
exercises.instruction: If a line is correct, write a dash (-). If there is an extra word, write that word.

items.prompt: I'm an only child. People often say to me: 'Wouldn't you be a lot
happier if you **have had** brothers or sisters?' but I don't see it like that.
It's true that if I **had had** a brother or sister, I would have someone closer
to my own age to talk to and play with at home, but I don't think that's
very important **provided** for you have close friends, which I do. If my
parents **would** have more children, they wouldn't be able to spend so much
time with me. And we have great fun together! **Also**, except if I had a
brother or sister, I'd have **it** to share a bedroom with them. That might be
fun, but what would happen if I wanted to play my CDs and **he** or she had
to study? No — I don't want a brother or sister, unless it **will** happens, of course. In that case, I'll think it's the best thing in the world!
